references.text: Isaiah prophesies about a future feast where the Lord will prepare a banquet with 'aged, clarified wine' – the best wine – for all peoples. Jesus serving the best wine at the end of the wedding in Cana points to this eschatological fulfillment ([ref:Jes 25:6|Isaiah 25:6]).

Jesus says: 'No one who has drunk old wine wants new; for they say, The old is good.' The steward's comment at Cana turns this expectation on its head – the best wine comes last, as a sign that what Jesus brings surpasses the old ([ref:Luk 5:39|Luke 5:39]).

Jesus speaks of new wine that must be put into new wineskins – the new cannot be contained by the old. The new, better wine at Cana corresponds to this image of how the new in God's kingdom surpasses the old ([ref:Mark 2:22|Mark 2:22]).

Amos prophesies about a coming time of abundance where 'the mountains will drip with sweet wine' and the people will again plant vineyards and drink wine. The good wine Jesus creates can be seen as a sign of this messianic fulfillment ([ref:Am 9:13-14|Amos 9:13-14]).

Joel prophesies about a day when 'the mountains will drip with sweet wine,' an image of the abundance of God's kingdom in the messianic age. Jesus' miracle of the good wine points forward to this fulfillment ([ref:Joel 3:18|Joel 3:18]).

John summarizes that this was the beginning of Jesus' signs, and that he revealed his glory. The good wine saved for last is itself the sign that reveals Jesus' divine glory ([ref:Joh 2:11|John 2:11]).
The psalmist praises God who gives 'wine that gladdens the human heart.' The good wine Jesus creates at the wedding reflects God's generous care and joy ([ref:Sal 104:15|Psalm 104:15]).
